prompt:
# Subject Merge Fine Clustering

## Quick Start

Inside one topic area, create tight candidate clusters that are worth a later same-concept decision. Use only the provided candidate cards.

## Identity Filter

Cluster candidates only when they might be the same teachable idea at the same level, testable with the same question.

Do not cluster just because candidates share a keyword. Keep candidates separate when one adds implementation, math, limitation, application, deeper mechanism, tool-specific behavior, or a broader/narrower student action.

Doubt means singleton. Under-clustering is safer than sending unrelated candidates to merge evaluation.

## Output

Return one JSON object only:

```json
{
  "clusters": [
    {
      "id": "cluster_001",
      "label": "Short candidate cluster",
      "rationale": "Why these candidates may share concept identity.",
      "candidate_ids": ["candidate-id"]
    }
  ]
}
```

## Self-Check

- Every input candidate ID appears exactly once.
- Each non-singleton cluster has a plausible same-concept reason.
- Implementation, limitation, application, math, and deeper-revisit candidates were not grouped with definitions just because labels overlap.
- Mixed-language same-level candidates were clustered when their teachable idea matches.
- No web search or external knowledge was used.

area.label: Neural Network Foundations and History
area.rationale: Historical and conceptual: McCulloch-Pitts, Hebbian learning, perceptron, ADALINE, AI winter, revival, and basic architectures (FF, RNN, LSTM, autoencoder, GAN, CNN, DRN). Also includes perceptron limitations and MLP intro.

candidates.label: McCulloch-Pitts neuron model
candidates.description: The first computational model of a neuron proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, representing neurons as simple electrical circuits with binary outputs.
coverage_criteria: Identify McCulloch and Pitts as the authors of the first formal neuron model in 1943.
Describe the basic idea of a simplified neuron with binary output.

candidates.label: Hebbian learning
candidates.description: The principle that neural connections are strengthened when the pre- and post-synaptic neurons fire together, introduced by Donald Hebb in 1949 and later formalized as a learning rule.
coverage_criteria: State Hebb's postulate: 'neurons that fire together wire together'.
Give one example of a Hebbian-like learning rule.

candidates.label: Perceptron
candidates.description: A single-layer neural network model by Frank Rosenblatt (1958) that computes a weighted sum of inputs, subtracts a threshold, and outputs a binary class; it defines a linear decision boundary.
coverage_criteria: Explain the perceptron architecture: inputs, weights, bias, activation (step function).
State that the perceptron performs binary classification and can learn simple linearly separable patterns.

candidates.label: ADALINE and MADALINE
candidates.description: Early adaptive linear neural networks (ADALINE, MADALINE) developed by Widrow and Hoff (1959) that used adaptive linear elements; MADALINE was the first neural network applied to a real-world problem (echo cancellation).
coverage_criteria: Explain what ADALINE and MADALINE stand for.
Identify echo cancellation as the first real-world application of a neural network (MADALINE).

candidates.label: Minsky & Papert critique and the AI winter
candidates.description: The 1969 book 'Perceptrons' by Minsky and Papert proved the limitations of single-layer perceptrons, leading to a halt in neural network funding and research throughout the 1970s.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Minsky and Papert demonstrated the inability of perceptrons to solve non-linearly separable problems (like XOR), causing a funding freeze.
Define the term 'AI winter' in the context of neural networks.

candidates.label: Hopfield networks and the revival of neural network research
candidates.description: John Hopfield's 1982 paper and the US-Japan Conference on Cooperative Competitive Neural Networks rekindled interest and funding in neural networks, ending the AI winter.
coverage_criteria: State that Hopfield's 1982 approach and the US-Japan conference helped restart neural network funding.
Mention that the conference and the Japanese fifth-generation project spurred renewed investment.

candidates.label: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
candidates.description: A specialized recurrent neural network architecture using gated memory cells (forget, input, output gates) to learn long-term dependencies and mitigate the vanishing gradient problem; introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997.
coverage_criteria: Explain the purpose of an LSTM: to handle long-term dependencies in sequences.
Name the three gates and their basic roles (forget, input, output).
Contrast LSTM with a simple RNN in terms of memory capability.

candidates.label: Feedforward neural network architecture
candidates.description: A neural network organized into sequential layers (input, hidden, output) where connections flow only forward without cycles; each neuron computes a weighted sum plus bias followed by an activation function.
coverage_criteria: Sketch a diagram of a feedforward network with at least one hidden layer.
Explain the function of weights and biases in a feedforward neuron.

candidates.label: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) basics
candidates.description: A neural network architecture with feedback connections that pass information from one time step to the next, creating an internal memory suitable for sequential data.
coverage_criteria: Explain how recurrent loops distinguish RNNs from feedforward networks.
Give an example of a task that benefits from recurrent architecture (e.g., language modeling, time series prediction).

candidates.label: Autoencoder
candidates.description: An unsupervised neural network that compresses input into a lower-dimensional representation (encoding) and reconstructs the original input (decoding), useful for dimensionality reduction and feature learning.
coverage_criteria: Sketch the encoder-bottleneck-decoder structure.
Explain how an autoencoder can be used for data compression or denoising.

candidates.label: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
candidates.description: A framework where a generator network creates synthetic data and a discriminator network tries to distinguish it from real data; adversarial training improves both.
coverage_criteria: Explain the roles of the generator and discriminator.
Describe the adversarial training process as a two-player game.

candidates.label: Convolutional Neural Networks
candidates.description: CNNs are architectures for grid-structured data (e.g., images) that use convolutional layers to detect spatial features, pooling layers to reduce dimensionality, and fully-connected layers for classification. Output size depends on input, filter, stride, and padding.
coverage_criteria: Describe the operation of a convolutional layer (filter, stride, feature map).
Compute the output size of a convolutional layer given input dimensions, filter size, and padding.

candidates.label: Deep Residual Networks
candidates.description: Deep Residual Networks (DRNs) use skip connections (residual blocks) to allow gradients to flow through very deep architectures, mitigating the vanishing gradient problem and enabling training of networks like ResNet.
coverage_criteria: Explain what a residual block is and why it helps train very deep networks.
Name a well-known residual network architecture.

candidates.label: Perceptron and Its Limitations
candidates.description: The perceptron is a single neuron with step activation: output = step(∑ w_i x_i + b). Its training rule: w = w + η (d - y) x. It only solves linearly separable problems; XOR requires a hidden layer (e.g., two-layer network computing AND and OR).
coverage_criteria: Write the perceptron forward pass and training update rule.
Explain why a single perceptron cannot solve XOR and how a hidden layer enables the solution.

candidates.label: Perceptron Multicamadas
candidates.description: Introdução ao perceptron multicamadas como uma extensão para resolver problemas não-linearmente separáveis.
coverage_criteria: O aluno deve diferenciar um perceptron simples de um multicamadas pela presença de camadas ocultas.
O aluno deve justificar a necessidade de camadas múltiplas para datasets não-lineares.

candidate_assignment_rule: Cluster only. Every input candidate ID must appear exactly once across clusters. Prefer tight clusters; topic overlap alone is not a cluster.

web_access_policy.instruction: Do not use web search or open URLs. Use only the provided candidate cards.
